sections.html:
The Recorder of Deeds sits at 55 East Court Street, 6th floor, Doylestown. Call 215-348-6209. Counter hours are weekdays, 7:45 a.m. to 4:15 p.m., yet anything you want recorded has to be in by 4 p.m. A package that lands after noon may roll to the next workday.

Real estate records go back to 1684, when William Penn founded the county. Beyond deeds and mortgages, the office handles as many as 25 other types of paper, among them subdivision plans, UCC filings, mausoleum and sewer permits and notary commissions. Records are preserved on microfiche, microfilm and PDF/A, and bound books are no longer produced.

The county assessment board works hand in hand with the Recorder. Its deed registry staff review each document and attach tax parcel labels before recording, so a deed with a wrong parcel number or an outdated owner name can get stuck at that desk.

The fee schedule assumes one parcel, four names and four pages. Each page past four adds $4, each name past four adds $1, and each parcel past the first adds $10. For the base price of a deed or mortgage, use the recording fee calculator linked on the county's site, built by the state recorders association. The Statement of Value form isn't counted as a fee page.

Bucks County extra recording charges, effective January 2026
ChargeAmount
Each page after the fourth$4
Each name after the fourth$1
Each parcel after the first$10
Official search per name or item for a court order$5
Special handling per document$25
Rejected document returned$10
Paper copy of a receipt$0.50
Credit card service fee3.0%

Make checks and money orders payable to the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds. Calculators leave out certified copies, and staff confirm the final total when the document is recorded. Call 215-348-6209 to verify an amount before you mail anything.

The rate is 2%, shared equally by the state and the local taxing bodies, and the Recorder collects it when you file. It applies to the value of the interest conveyed, which can differ from the sale price. State and local rules are silent on who pays, so most purchase agreements split it between buyer and seller. If the amount paid falls short, the new owner is the one who owes the difference.

Since January 2026 the office refuses personal checks for transfer tax. It takes cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card. Title agents usually deal with this at settlement, so ask your closer which method will be used.

  • Some transfers are exempt, including conveyances between spouses, from parents to children, across three generations, and among siblings.
  • A one-time transfer between former spouses is allowed.
  • If an investigator finds a higher value, the state can bill extra tax and interest and mails the determination to you directly.
  • State revenue officials put their share at 1% of the value, collected along with any local tax by the county recorder.

You need the state's REV-183 Statement of Value whenever transfer tax isn't paid or the true value is missing from the deed, as with a $1 consideration. The form either sets the value or gives the reason for an exemption. Bucks accepts only the June 2019 version, and a paper copy must come in duplicate.

The form relies on the Common Level Ratio Factor, which the county posts for July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2027. State investigators may later test whether the stated value or exemption holds up. If it falls short, the state issues a determination, collects the extra tax and interest, and sends a receipt to the Recorder for recording.

When a deed is e-recorded, attachments such as a trust agreement, mortgage or assignment add a $1 per page copy fee. The office prints them for the Department of Revenue and then removes them from the public record. Sending those pages on paper avoids the charge.

Three routes work: e-record through Simplifile, CSC or ePN, carry the paper deed to the counter, or mail it. A mailed package needs the right checks payable to the Recorder and a stamped envelope addressed to yourself. Deeds, mortgages, general powers of attorney, satisfactions and copy requests go straight to the Recorder's office.

Book and page numbers ended on July 1, 2012, so every recorded document carries only an instrument number. Paper receipts ended that year too. Receipts now come by email, which requires the Submitter Information Form on file with the office.

  • The Fraud Alert System is free and tells an owner when something is recorded against the property.
  • A free email copy of your own deed is available on request.
  • Military discharge papers (DD-214) are recorded free.
  • An in-office notary is available.

Bucks covers 622 square miles between the Delaware River and Montgomery County, with Doylestown as the seat and Bensalem as the largest township. The 2020 population was 646,538. The median value of an owner-occupied home for 2020 to 2024 is $445,700, and 77.8% of households own their homes.

At that price, a 2% transfer tax is a real line item, so agree early on who bears it. Check that the municipality named on the deed matches the tax bill, since the local half of the tax depends on it. Ownership questions can go to the assessment board at 215-348-6219, though its public site can lag behind recordings.

Give your closing agent the parcel number, every owner name and the school district well ahead of settlement. The county has 54 townships and boroughs, and a short checklist of those three details can head off a rejected filing and the $10 return charge.

Gather the signed deed, the Statement of Value if tax is unpaid or the value is missing, and checks or a card for the fee. Confirm the parcel count and the number of names and pages so the charge is right the first time. Decide how the transfer tax will be paid, remembering that personal checks are refused. Choose e-recording, counter or mail, and meet the 4 p.m. cutoff, with noon as the safer mark. If you mail it, include a stamped return envelope and, if you want a receipt by email, the Submitter Information Form.

faqs.q: What are the Bucks County Recorder of Deeds office hours?
faqs.a: Counter service runs weekdays, 7:45 a.m. to 4:15 p.m. Documents to be recorded have to be submitted by 4 p.m. A package received after noon may wait for the next workday.

faqs.q: Can I pay Bucks County transfer tax with a personal check?
faqs.a: No. Since January 2026 the Recorder of Deeds refuses personal checks for realty transfer tax. Accepted methods are cash in the office, a cashier's check, a money order or a credit card, and cards carry a 3.0% service fee.

faqs.q: What is the fee for each extra page on a Bucks County deed?
faqs.a: Each page after the fourth costs $4. Names after the fourth cost $1 each and parcels after the first cost $10 each. The REV-183 Statement of Value isn't counted as a fee page.

faqs.q: Does Bucks County require a Statement of Value?
faqs.a: Yes, when transfer tax isn't paid or the deed lacks the true value, for example a $1 consideration. Use the June 2019 version of REV-183, in duplicate if submitted on paper. The state may later send a determination if the stated value looks low.

faqs.q: How far back do Bucks County deed records go?
faqs.a: The Recorder of Deeds holds records from 1684 to the present, kept on microfiche, microfilm and PDF/A. Documents recorded since July 1, 2012 carry an instrument number only.
